title: Playback keys
text: Media Player mode only for the transport keys — live capture has no position to seek or pause. The chrome keys (↑ / F1 / Esc) and N work in video processor mode as well. Every binding is an ordinary key inside the Unplugged window: nothing is captured while another app has focus, so Unplugged never interferes with anything else running on the machine. Key Action Space / Enter pause / resume ← / → back / forward 10 s; Shift = 60 s. While paused, one frame per press PgUp / PgDn previous / next chapter Home / End start / end of the title 0 – 9 jump to 0 % – 90 % of the title ↑ or F1 show / hide the full chrome + / − or ↓ volume up / down M mute N NLS on / off (same as the transport-bar button) S stop back to the library Ctrl+S save the current frame as PNG (paused only) Esc close settings → stop back to the library → recover the chrome, one layer per press Alt+F4 asks before closing

title: How to get started
text: Quick config Press F1 to open the live status and settings panels (or Up while something is playing); Esc closes them again. Convert to SDR — On. SDR display nits , Static nits (max) and Display black (nits) — set to your display's calibrated, measured values. The user trims — Exposure , Shadow detail , Contrast — live on the HDR tab. Leave the Zion tab settings on Auto where applicable. Calibration LUT files load from Output → Display calibration . Frame captures come from Output → Save frame as PNG (asks where), or Ctrl+S while the picture is paused, which writes straight to Pictures\Unplugged\<date>\frame_NNNN.png — one folder per day, numbered so captures never overwrite each other. The shortcut does nothing while playing: pause first so the frame is the one you are looking at. Why that order — three stages, in sequence: Calibration settings first. The tone curve maps HDR into your display's measured range. A wrong white, black or peak means every downstream decision is made for a display you don't own. These numbers are set once per display and never used for taste. If you have a measured calibration LUT , load it at this stage. Zion grade second. With Mode: Auto and the Band

title: How the panel works
text: Open the settings panel and pick a tab on the left icon rail: ▶ Playback · ⬡ Source · ◑ HDR · ✦ Zion · ▣ Output · ≡ System . Each tab is split into sections . Sections are an accordion: click a header to open it; only one section is open at a time. A tab with a single section (Source, System) is always open. Toggles flip ON/OFF with one click. Option rows ( ‹ value › ) cycle through their choices — click the right side to advance. Sliders are dragged on the bar; hover the bar and use the mouse wheel for one step of that row (1 on whole-number rows; the row's own increment on decimals — 0.01 on most, 0.05 on NLS Curve, 0.001 on Display black) — this is how you land on a measured value like 174 nits. With the panel focused, ←/→ move the row focus; ↑ stays the chrome toggle everywhere, including here. Everything applies live to the running picture and is saved immediately — including Convert to SDR and the debug passthroughs, which reselect the converter/shader in place rather than rebuilding the pipeline. Your settings are plain text at %LOCALAPPDATA%\Unplugged\s3_shell.ini . Every row writes itself there on first start, so you can back it up, or hand-edit a value a slider can't reac

title: Presets
text: A preset is a saved snapshot of the rows that describe the picture — tone curve and trims, the Zion grade, Output scalers, Geometry and non-linear stretch — plus the System switches that are not UI-only. It does not contain the Playback or Source tabs (see below). It is how you keep, say, a Projector setup and a Daylight TV setup side by side instead of re-tuning when the room or the display changes. First start: the app creates five presets — Preset 1 … Preset 5 — and makes Preset 1 active. On an upgrade they are seeded from your existing settings, so nothing changes on screen; on a fresh install they start from the compiled defaults. Rename them as you like. The active preset's name is shown in the title strip as Preset Name ▾ . Click it to open the preset card. In the card What it does The list Default first, then your presets alphabetically. Click a preset to switch to it — it applies immediately, and the card stays open so you can click through several to compare them on the same frame. New Asks for a name (pre-filled Preset 1 , Preset 2 …) and creates a preset that starts as a copy of the one you are using — tune once, name it, and it is yours from then on. Rename Same settin

title: Default is read-only — and custom presets save themselves
text: Default is locked. Trying to change any picture row while it is active is refused — the control does not move — and a warning appears in the centre of the screen , "Default is read-only — Default is the locked baseline: picture changes are refused while it is active. Switch to a preset, or create one, to change anything." , which stays until you press OK (Enter or Esc also dismiss it). The N key behaves the same way. That is deliberate: Default is the compiled baseline, so what you see there is always repeatable. To start working, switch to a preset or create one with New — a new preset starts as a copy of the current values, so nothing is lost. Exception — Playback and Source. The Playback and Source tabs are never locked and never part of a preset. Choosing the audio mode, an input device, rescanning ports or running first-time setup is a property of the machine and the session, not of a look — so it stays available on Default , and a preset never drags the input along with it. Exception — the display rows. SDR display nits , Static nits (max) , Display black (nits) , Convert to SDR and Output gamut describe the screen you calibrated, not a look, so they are never part of a prese

title: What a preset does not contain
text: Five rows describe the display you calibrated, not your taste , so they stay with the machine and switching presets never changes them — and, as above, they are always editable, even on Default : SDR display nits · Static nits (max) · Display black (nits) · Convert to SDR · Output gamut Also not part of a preset: the Playback and Source tabs (audio mode, input device, setup), the two UI-only rows on the System tab (context banner, auto-next), and the playback position. Those belong to the app and the session, not to a look. The other System switches (automatic update check, tray icon) are ordinary rows and do travel with a preset. One behaviour worth knowing: the preset you last used is re-applied when the next picture comes up (the first play or capture after launch), after the base settings file has loaded. So a preset's value wins over a hand-edit you made in s3_shell.ini — change the row while that preset is active (it saves itself) or switch to Default first.

title: Playback (media files)
text: The Playback tab is dimmed and unreachable during live capture — its controls address the file-playing pipeline, which capture never builds.

title: Audio
text: Setting Choices Default What it does Track every audio stream in the file first track Picks the language/format. Names come from the file itself: "Deutsch TrueHD Atmos 7.1". HD audio Bitstream / PCM Bitstream Bitstream : the compressed audio (Dolby, DTS, TrueHD, Atmos) is passed untouched to your receiver, which decodes it and shows its logo. PCM : the PC decodes it first — use this if the receiver can't decode the format, or to hear everything through TV speakers. Bitstream is the shipped default: an AVR decodes its own formats better than a PC downmix. Delay −500…+500 ms 0 Intended for lip-sync correction. In this version the slider saves but nothing reacts to it yet — it has no effect.

title: Subtitles
text: Setting Choices Default What it does Track Off / every subtitle stream Off Picks the subtitle track. Names keep the format in brackets — (SRT) etc. — because only text subtitles can be styled; bitmap ones (PGS, VobSub) are images and always look how the disc made them.

title: Source (live capture)
text: One row per physical DeckLink input, plus three actions. Row Shows What it does Port row name + badge Click to switch the player to that HDMI input. The active port gets ● . Badges: 🔒 HDR PQ = an HDR signal is locked and being carried, 🔒 Dolby Vision = a Dolby Vision source (the card cannot flag DV, so this is read from its signature — BT.2020 colours with an SDR range flag, and confirmed by the picture being a PQ base layer without static mastering metadata), 🔒 HDR HLG = HLG, ○ no signal = nothing is plugged in or the source is off, — unknown = signal present but not identified yet. ⟳ Rescan inputs — Re-asks the card what is plugged in. Use after connecting a new device. ✎ Rename inputs… — Names your ports ("Console", "Bluray") — the name is yours only; the underlying input is unchanged. ▶ First-time setup… (restarts app) — Restarts the app into the setup wizard. Stops any playback.

title: HDR tab
text: Everything here shapes how an HDR signal arrives on your display, plus a few post-processing tools. SDR display nits and the Display Target numbers are set once — they describe your display, not your taste — and day to day most people only touch Tone curve , Exposure and the taste sliders.

title: Tone Mapping
text: Setting Choices / range Default What it does Convert to SDR On / Off On On: HDR video is tone-mapped into the normal (SDR) range this app renders. Off: the HDR signal is passed on for your TV itself to map — only sensible with an HDR-capable TV in HDR mode. When Off, everything else in this tab and the Zion tab stops mattering, because this app is no longer doing the picture. SDR display nits 25…400 80 The measured SDR white luminance of your display — a calibration number like Static nits (max) below, never a taste knob. Enter your measured value (a TV in a bright room typically 100–200; a projector in the dark 40–80) and leave it there. What a wrong number does: declared below your measurement, the picture runs bright and the highlights pay — the shoulder clips sooner and sky detail goes first; declared above it, films render dark with headroom unused. Brightness without lying about your panel is what Exposure is for. Tone curve Unplugged / GT7 Adapt Unplugged How HDR's brightness range is squeezed into your display's. Unplugged — the house curve, and the safe choice for everything Dolby Vision: DV carries its own per-scene mastering and this curve respects it. GT7 Adapt — the ho

title: Curve Settings (appears only for GT7 Adapt )
text: Setting Range Default What it does Title peak (nits) 100…4000 1000 The content peak the curve squeezes from. Leave at 1000 unless you know the disc's MaxCLL. Auto exposure On / Off Off Solves the working peak from each scene's measured average instead of guessing (updates at scene cuts, never mid-shot). Use when a title looks consistently a third of a stop off. Exposure target 0.20…0.70 0.42 With Auto exposure On: where the scene average should land (0 = black, 1 = white). GT7 blend (ch<->UCS) 0…1 0.6 How much highlights keep their source colour: 0 = curve re-derives it, 1 = source colour returned intact. GT7 chroma fade from 0.3…2.0 0.98 The level where that colour blend starts. Default leaves it a highlights-only move. GT7 adapt to scene peak 0…1 0.25 How far the peak moves from Title peak toward the measured scene peak. Raise for sources without usable metadata (HDMI consoles, streaming apps). GT7 desaturation 0…1 0 Colour pulled out of highlights only , in proportion to how hard they were compressed. Mid-tones and skin are untouched. GT7 shoulder reach 0.02…0.90 0.25 Highlight headroom: lower = longer shoulder , more brightness band survives before detail merges to white; highe

title: Display Target
text: These describe your TV/projector , not the content. Set once per display. Setting Range Default What it does Windows HDR Do not change / On (fullscreen) / On / On/off (fullscreen) / On/off Do not change Whether this app toggles Windows' own HDR mode for the display when playing. Leave Do not change if you set HDR/SDR mode in Windows yourself; the others switch it for you at playback start (the "on/off" pair restores your previous state afterwards). Static nits (max) 10…1000 1000 Your display's measured peak white in SDR mode. This is the destination the tone curve maps to — get it wrong and everything is wrong. Measured 174 on a projector? Type nothing: drag near it, then mouse-wheel over the bar, 1 nit per click. A display brighter than 1000 nits: edit hdr.maxNits in the INI directly (the engine accepts up to 10000). Display black (nits) 0…2 0 Your display's measured black level. At 0 the curve assumes a perfect black and spends shadow detail on range you can't actually see. A projector measuring 0.3: enter 0.3 — the destination range starts there and the shadow band is redistributed into what the panel shows. For OLED (true black), 0 is right. Subtitle/OSD brightness 0…100 0 How

title: Post-FX
text: These run after tone mapping and grading, on the final image — they behave identically on SDR, HDR10 and Dolby Vision sources. Setting Choices / range Default What it does Adaptive sharpen On / Off Off Edge-adaptive detail: measures each edge against its local neighbourhood and limits itself, so it adds detail without white halos. Soft SD/HD sources benefit; clean 4K rarely needs it. Sharpen strength 0.3…1.5 1.0 How much of that adaptive detail to add. 0.3 is a whisper, 1.0 strong and still safe, ~1.2+ starts showing its hand on film grain. Deband On / Off On Removes the stepped bands that appear in slow gradients (sky fades, dark walls) — the banding the 10→8-bit conversion creates — by flattening each band edge then covering the work with fine grain. On by default; only turn it off if you would rather keep the grain exactly as encoded. Deband threshold 0…256 32 How small a gradient step gets treated; pushing it high starts eating real picture detail. Deband range 1…64 16 How wide an area is blended per band. Deband iterations 1…4 1 Processing passes; 2 is usually the honest maximum. Deband grain 0…128 24 The noise that hides the blending — 0 exposes it as mush; matching real film

title: Zion tab — the grade
text: The Zion pipeline models your display and content and corrects both. One switch owns the whole tab, and there's a one-click undo for a session gone wrong. Setting Default What it does Enable ML grade On The master switch for everything on this tab. Off = the render is pure tone curve + post-FX; every section below becomes decorative. Turning it on while Mode is Off also sets Mode to Auto — the switch is the master, and it says so in the row above it. ⟲ Reset grade to defaults — Asks, then restores every row on this tab to its factory value. The quickest way out of a grade you can't diagnose.

title: Tone Curve
text: Setting Range Default What it does Band controller On/Off On The closed loop. Instead of applying shadow/gamma/highlight corrections blindly, it solves all three together every frame so the delivered picture lands on fixed house levels (deep shadow, mid, and highlight anchors). While it's On, it owns the legacy Shadow slider and the manual Gamma top-up — those stand down because applying them on top would double the move. Off returns you to the older, open-loop path (the sliders below act directly again). Mode Auto / Manual / Off Auto Auto : the scene model judges shadow toe, gamma and highlight per scene and applies the corrections itself. Manual : the model's per-scene gamma freezes and the sliders become the sole authority — this is the starting point for manual tuning. Off : the tone-curve leg of the grade does nothing; micro-contrast and the rest still run. Shadow 0…0.40 0 A legacy multiplicative toe on the dark end. Effective in Manual mode with the Band controller Off (otherwise the controller's own solution overrides it — see its row). Positive opens blacks progressively; past ~0.15 you will start seeing it everywhere , because a toe lift is global, not local. Shadow dehaze

title: Chroma
text: Colour saturation shaping — how vivid a colour gets, with a brake for skin. (Note: the "Mode" row on this section currently saves but nothing acts on it; the Default behaviour is what always runs.) Setting Range Default What it does Normal 1.0…1.3 1.08 Chroma gain for ordinary-saturation colours: skin, foliage, interiors. The small default boost is the house vividness; 1.0 is pass-through. Fire 1.0…1.3 1.15 Chroma gain for the hottest band — flames, neon, emissives — where extra saturation reads as heat rather than error. Knee 0.1…0.9 0.45 Where "ordinary" stops and "fire" begins, as a saturation level. Lower classifies more of the image into the hot band. Skin 0.5…1.0 0.95 The skin brake: what fraction of the boost faces are allowed. 1.0 = faces get the full push, 0.5 = half. Guards against actors going lobster-orange.

title: Micro Contrast
text: Local clarity — texture inside objects, not edge sharpening. Runs on its own enable switch even if the tone-curve Mode is Off. Setting Range Default What it does Enable On/Off On Switches the micro-contrast engine. Strength 0…0.5 0.15 How much local contrast to recover. The effect is texture-gated: flat gradients are left alone, real structure gets pushed. Past ~0.3 surfaces mastering noise and grain noise as "detail". Zone lo 0…0.6 0.15 The brightness floor where the engine works at all. Everything below (night scenes' true blacks) is skipped — low-luma is where local contrast invents dirt. Raise it if dark scenes get mottled. Ratio cap 1.0…2.0 1.4 The halo limiter: the maximum contrast ratio one pixel's neighbourhood may be pushed to. Lower = gentler, no rims; higher = stronger effect, but >1.7 on hard edges is where halos come from. Skin protect 0…1 0.65 Faces get only this fraction of the effect — the difference between "pores" and "stubble texture on a model".

title: Debug
text: Diagnostics for finding out why the picture is what it is. Leave every row here Off for normal viewing. Setting What it does HDR passthrough Bypasses this app's entire picture pipeline and hands the raw signal to the display — the "is it the renderer or the TV" test. Applies immediately (it swaps the shader the render loop binds, with no pipeline rebuild). On a non-HDR display you'll see flat/green-grey nonsense; that's expected, not broken. Mutually exclusive with the next row by design. Tone curve passthrough Skips the Zion ML grade and nothing else: the picture is what the tone curve alone delivers — HDR converted to SDR by the selected curve, no per-scene model, no grade. It applies live. This is the A/B for the grade : if the picture is right here and wrong with the grade on, the grade is the suspect; if it is already wrong here, the tone curve or the display side is. Also auto-switches HDR passthrough off. Frame log Writes a verbose per-frame telemetry line to the engine log ( %USERPROFILE%\.unplugged\logs\engine.log ) — what each stage computed, frame by frame. The thing to turn on when asking "why did the picture change there". MC heat Replaces the picture with a greyscale

title: Black Bars
text: Setting Default What it does Repaint bars Off Overwrites the letterbox mattes with true black every frame. For sources whose "black" bars carry lifted noise or crawl; clean masters don't need it and it's extra GPU work. Highlight bars Off Tints the detected bar regions so you can see what the app thinks is black bar — the way to verify detection before trusting Repaint.

title: Sky Seg
text: Experimental, off by default: the ML segmentor (ONNX/YOLO) carves the frame into sky regions so their highlight treatment can differ from the rest. If you did not go looking for this, leave it off. Setting Choices / range Default What it does Enable On / Off Off Switches the sky segmentor on. Off leaves the picture untouched. Strength 0…1 0.6 How much the sky region's special treatment is applied there. Mask overlay On / Off Off Diagnostic: paints the detected sky mask so you can see what it locked onto.

title: Person Skin
text: Experimental, off by default: segments people so faces can be protected while the rest of the frame is graded. Setting Choices / range Default What it does Enable On / Off Off Switches the person segmentor on. Strength 0…1 1.0 How fully the detected region is treated as skin. Mask overlay On / Off Off Diagnostic: paints the detected people mask. Tone preserve 0…1 0 How much of a face's original tone survives the grade — raise it to pull skin back toward the source while the rest of the frame stays graded.

title: Video Processing
text: Setting Choices / range Default What it does Super Resolution On/Off Off The renderer's upscaler for small sources: SD/HD material on a 4K panel gets a genuine reconstruction pass instead of plain interpolation. Turning it On also enables the two plumbing switches it needs (behind the scenes, no action from you). Know its limits: it doesn't engage for 10-bit or HDR sources, needs RTX-class NVIDIA or Intel graphics, and a 4K source on a 4K display has nothing to upscale. Windows' and the NVIDIA panel's own settings are outside this app's reach. Chroma upsampling CatmullRom / KrigBilateral KrigBilateral How colour from 4:2:0 video (almost all of it) is expanded to full resolution. CatmullRom is the cheaper, always-safe filter; KrigBilateral reconstructs chroma edges from the luma (best on fine colour detail like red subtitle text) at noticeably more GPU cost. Upscaling Lanczos3 / Jinc2 Jinc2 The enlargement filter for smaller-than-display sources. Jinc2 is the sharper reconstruction (the default, best for SD/HD onto 4K); Lanczos3 is a touch calmer, with less ringing on hard edges and grain. On noisy material, sharper is not better. Downscaling Lanczos / BicubicSharp Lanczos Shrinking

title: Geometry
text: Setting Choices / range Default What it does Fit mode Source / Fixed aspect / Fill screen Source How the picture is fitted to the window. Source respects the video's own aspect; Fixed aspect uses the Fixed aspect value; Fill screen stretches to the window and can remove black bars. Fixed aspect 1.00 – 3.00 1.78 The display aspect used in Fixed aspect mode. 1.78 = 16:9, 2.39 = scope. For a 2.35 screen use the screen's measured ratio. Zoom 50 – 200 % 100 % Scales the fitted picture. Above 100 % crops the overflow; use with Pan. 100 % is the neutral fit. Pan X -100 – 100 % 0 % Moves a zoomed picture horizontally across its overflow. Has no effect while the picture fits inside the window. Pan Y -100 – 100 % 0 % Moves a zoomed picture vertically across its overflow. Has no effect while the picture fits inside the window.

title: Non-linear stretch
text: A separate section in the rail, below Geometry . Everything here applies live, including on a paused frame — the geometry moves with the sliders and with N . That is deliberate: it is the only practical way to judge the sweet spot. Setting Choices / range Default What it does Enable NLS On/Off Off Non-linear stretch: expands the active picture toward the screen edges while keeping the central band close to its original geometry. Intended for scope screens, projectors and anamorphic setups. Off by default; switching it on with the stock settings fills a letterboxed scope title immediately — the rows below are for tuning that result, not for making it happen. Bars removed 0 – 100 % 100 % How much of the letterbox the picture grows into. 0 shows it at its own aspect (bars untouched, no distortion); 100 fills the screen. The correction the fill costs scales with it — taking half the bars costs half the distortion — so this is the "how many of the black bars do I get rid of" dial. Whatever is left can be zoomed away, which spends side picture instead of shape. Axis Horizontal / Vertical / Split Horizontal Which axis carries the aspect correction. Horizontal keeps the height untouched (

title: Output (statistics & frame capture)
text: Setting Choices / range Default What it does Show statistics On/Off Off The renderer's on-screen performance overlay — frame render intervals, dropped frames, GPU figures. What to turn on when asking "is it smooth". Save frame as PNG button — Captures the exact frame the renderer drew (not a screen grab: no overlays, no desktop compositing, no colour shift from screen capture) and lets you file it as lossless PNG. The right tool for showing someone a picture question.

title: Display Calibration
text: Setting Choices / range Default What it does Calibration LUT file picker unset Loads a display-calibration .cube (e.g. from DisplayCAL) applied as the final pass — it shapes what your panel actually emits, separate from tone mapping which shapes the signal. Clearing (mode → Off) frees the texture. LUT mode Off / Gamma only / Greyscale / Full 3D Full 3D How much of the loaded cube to honour. Gamma only: the neutral lightness curve (for a display whose colour balance is already set). Greyscale: per-channel tone and balance, no channel mixing. Full 3D: everything, including the gamut remap — the complete calibration, with the caveat that 3D cubes gently fade deep saturated colours.

title: App
text: Setting Choices Default What it does Check for updates automatically On / Off On Asks GitHub for the latest release once a day, in the background. When something newer exists, a card appears at start with the release notes and a link to the download page. Off stops the automatic check; Check for updates now still works. Check for updates now button — Runs the check immediately and always reports: a newer version opens its card, otherwise a short "you are on the latest version" message. Also useful after installing on a machine that has been offline. Report a problem button — The support action for a picture or playback problem. Not wired in this build — it only writes a line to the log. Show context banner for settings On / Off On Draws the short explanation banner above the rows while you move around the panel. Off gives more rows on screen once you know the controls. Play next item automatically On / Off On When a title ends, offers the next episode/film in the library after a five-second countdown; Esc (or the card's Cancel) stops it. Off returns to the library at the end of the title. Show IMDb ratings On / Off On Draws the IMDb rating chip on posters and in detail rows. Rating

title: Recipes — start here
text: "Everything looks dim." Check SDR display nits holds your display's measured white — a number above the measurement is exactly what renders every film dark, and the fix is the honest number, not a darker one. Still dim at the measured value → Exposure (+1 = one-third stop; pre-curve, the shoulder absorbs it). A specific film still off on GT7 Adapt → Auto exposure On. "Bright scenes hurt / whites glare." Pull Exposure down; GT7 Adapt users whose explosions lose detail → GT7 shoulder reach down (0.25→0.15). Don't reach for SDR display nits — that row carries your display's measured white and stays there. "Skies are neon / garish blues." Gamut capacity (709) down to ~0.6; GT7 curves: GT7 desaturation 0.3–0.6. Unplugged curve with grade On: Highlight desat ~0.5. "Blacks are grey / no depth." Check Display black (nits) matches a measured value (a 0.3-black projector told "0 perfect" wastes shadow range). Auto mode: Shadow dehaze up (it strips the model's safety lift). Too much texture in shadows → Shadow detail down. "The image feels flat." Contrast +1…+2, or Micro Contrast Strength 0.15→0.25. Both at once is usually one too many. "Faces look waxy/oily." Every texture enhancer is a susp

title: Current limitations
text: Playback → Delay (audio lip-sync) saves but does nothing yet. Zion → Chroma → Mode saves but does nothing yet; the Default behaviour always runs. System → Report a problem saves a log line only; no report is sent. Super Resolution is not available for HDR or 10-bit sources; it is a SDR-path feature. With strong non-linear stretch, fine text can look slightly soft — both axes are being resampled when Axis = Split . Lower Strength or Centre protection if it bothers you. Disc images (ISO) and BDMV folder playback are not supported; rip to a file. Subtitle styling (font, size, colour) is not in this panel; only track selection is.

title: unplugged — open-source HDR tone mapping software for Windows
text: Free · Open source · Home cinema video processor Cinema-grade HDR tone mapping. Open source. Real time. Unplugged bridges the gap — scene-by-scene tone mapping, three ML models, and a picture you can actually tune. Free, open source, runs on your HTPC. Download free How it works Windows 10/11 · 127 MB · No subscription · No account “Unplugged + Zion on default settings looked better than my tuned madVR setup.” — AVS Forum user Unplugged 2.1.0 Media Player · real screenshot Works with Unencrypted HDMI PC & camera output Projectors OLED & QLED TVs MKV & MP4 Plug in and play Three steps to a better picture. No subscription, no cloud account, no installer labyrinth. Set it up once and leave it alone. 01 Install on your PC One 127 MB download for Windows 10 or 11. The installer brings the runtime it needs, so there is nothing else to fetch. 02 Point it at your movie library Media Player mode needs no capture card. Open your films, choose a track and watch — MKV, MP4, HEVC and TrueHD/Atmos are handled natively. 03 Add live HDMI When you want consoles, cameras or PC output, add a DeckLink card and Blackmagic's Desktop Video runtime. Unplugged locks the signal and applies the tone map and grade. Live HDMI needs an unencrypted source and Blackmagic's free Desktop Video runtime, installed separately — Unplugged does not bundle it. Most people start with Media Player mode and add a capture card later. One video processor, every source Live TV, movies and games — one picture. An unencrypted HDMI source and a file on disk get the same tone mapping, the same picture controls and the same calibration. The only difference is where the picture comes from. Picture pipeline DeckLink · files 01 HDMI input 4K HDR10 · HLG · Dolby Vision Live 02 Tone mapping Unplugged default · GT7 Adapt 2 curves 03 Zion Grade Shadow · mid-tone · highlight 3 models 04 Calibration Optional DisplayCAL .cube Final pass 05 Display BT.709 SDR · your measured target Out The same five stages run for live HDMI and files. Live HDMI An unencrypted HDMI source — just press play Plug an unencrypted source into the PC and Unplugged takes it from there. SDR, HDR10, HLG and Dolby Vision are recognised automatically. 4K HDR from an unencrypted source you control Name your inputs: Camera, PC, Console Switch sources in one click, without leaving the picture More about live HDMI → Media player Your movie library, the same great picture Play your own films with the same renderer, the same tone mapping and the same calibration as live HDMI. MKV, MP4 and the usual formats; HEVC and AVC video TrueHD/Atmos, DTS-HD and AC-3; bitstream or PCM SRT, ASS, SSA, PGS and VobSub subtitles, right in the picture A library with posters, ratings and episode artwork Requirements and download → Video Processor or Media Player? Both modes run the same picture pipeline. The difference is where the picture comes from. Choose your setup Video Processor Media Player Picture source Live HDMI from an unencrypted source Your own MKV, MP4 and similar files Capture hardware DeckLink card + Desktop Video runtime None Best for Consoles, cameras, PC output Films you already own Picture pipeline Tone mapping · Zion Grade · LUT The same pipeline Setup Pick the input once Point it at a folder How Unplugged compares Different approach. Different price. The dedicated processors are mature, and they lead on turnkey hardware, latency, geometry and dealer support. Unplugged leads on learned grading, price and openness. Here is the honest split. title: Dynamic HDR tone mapping for home cinema — unplugged
text: unplugged / HDR picture Dynamic tone mapping HDR that looks right in your room. Unplugged maps HDR10, HLG and Dolby Vision to your projector or TV, scene by scene, then lets you tune the look without breaking the picture. Download free Fine-tune your screen → The short version: Unplugged reads the HDR signal, measures each scene, and maps it to the brightness and black level your display can actually show. You choose a look, set your screen once, and the picture stays right. How the picture is built Every stage runs inside the same app, so there is no separate toolchain to keep in sync. Input. Your live HDMI source or movie file comes in. Tone mapping. HDR is mapped into the brightness range your display can show, using the source's own information where it has it. Picture tuning. Shadow, mid and highlight are balanced for the scene, then your trims apply on top. Calibration. Your screen's own correction is applied last. The status readout shows the peak currently in use, so you can see what the picture is working from. Two looks, one default Unplugged is the house curve and the default for every HDR source, Dolby Vision included. It is the safe choice: a Dolby Vision signal carries its own scene-by-scene information, and the curve respects it. GT7 Adapt is the manual choice for HDR10 and HLG. It uses the title's own peak brightness, together with each scene, to place the highlights. The picture controls work identically on both curves. Unplugged Default · every HDR source · Dolby Vision GT7 Adapt Manual · HDR10 and HLG · title MaxCLL + scene peak Taste trims Exposure · Shadow detail · Contrast · both curves What the source tells it HDR10 can carry static metadata: MaxCLL, MaxFALL and the mastering display. When it is present, the title's MaxCLL sizes the highlight ceiling instead of a generic assumption. Metadata is read from live capture when the card carries it and from files when the container has it. Dolby Vision over HDMI is its own case. The card marks such a signal with BT.2020 colour and no ordinary HDR flag, so the app identifies it by that signature rather than falling back to SDR, and reports it as Dolby Vision in the input dialog and the Info panel. When a source carries no usable metadata, the grade works from a measured scene peak. The peak in use is visible on the status readout, so “why is the picture mapped like this?” has an answer on screen. Set your screen up once Three numbers describe your screen. Set them once from a calibration report and leave them; changing them to make one film look brighter moves every film. Control What it is SDR display nits Where diffuse white sits on your display. A TV in a bright room is typically 100–200; a projector in a dark room 40–80. Static nits (max) Your display's measured peak white. This is the destination the curve maps to. Display black Your display's measured black level, so shadow detail is not spent on a black the panel cannot show. OLED at true black is 0; a projector measuring 0.3 gets 0.3. Declaring SDR white below your measurement makes the picture run bright and the shoulder clips sooner. Declaring it above makes films render dark with headroom unused. If a specific film looks wrong, Exposure is the dial for that; the display numbers are not. Easy picture controls Zero is an exact no-op on every trim, so a look you like is never disturbed by a dial you did not touch. Exposure −5…+5 · input gain in thirds of a stop, applied before the curve so the shoulder absorbs it instead of clipping. Shadow detail −5…+5 · spreads dark values apart without lifting true black. Detail, not brightness. Contrast −5…+5 · a symmetric S-curve about mid grey; black, mid and white stay exactly put. Highlight desat 0…1 · pulls saturation toward the level's neutral point, hue preserved. Guards the cyan cast HDR masters carry into dusk skies. Gamut capacity 0.20…1.00 · lands out-of-gamut colour at a fraction of its distance to the display edge. Pale colours stay untouched. Scene by scene, not shot by shot A band controller solves shadow, mid and highlight together every frame so the delivered picture lands on fixed house anchors. Exposure is treated as a property of the scene, not the shot: the model updates at scene cuts and never mid-shot, so an approved change lands in one frame rather than drifting through a scene. Above that sit corrections you can reach for when a title needs them: shadow dehaze pulls back the model's own safety lift on dark scenes; highlight shoulder softens or tightens the roll-off; mid-tone target solves the gamma that lands the scene average where you asked; chroma has a skin brake; micro-contrast is texture-gated and halo-limited. The Zion Grade Three real-time machine-learning models read every frame and predict how a colourist would shape the tone curve for that scene: one for shadow, one for mid-tone, one for highlight. Their combined inference drives the Zion Grade, so the picture tracks the scene rather than a single curve set at the start. Auto is the default. Manual freezes the per-scene gamma and puts the sliders in charge. The picture controls above work on top either way, and zero remains an exact no-op. In development: GPU-based sky and skin segmentation, intended to protect faces and complex gradients under aggressive tone curves. It is an open research pipeline, not part of the shipped picture yet. Calibration is the final polish The tone mapper describes the signal. The calibration LUT describes the panel. Keeping them separate means a new display measurement does not require re-tuning the grade, and a grade you like survives a recalibration. A DisplayCAL .cube loads as the final pass with its own enable toggle, so you can A/B the correction without unloading the file. What it will not do: Dolby Vision profile 5 in a file is not supported in Media Player mode. Dolby Vision over HDMI is recognised and handled. ISO and BDMV folder playback are not supported; rip to a file first. Map it to your screen. Free · GPL-3.0 · Windows 10/11 x64 Download unplugged

Unplugged locks the signal, recognises the format and presents it full-screen with your picture applied. Download free What happens to the picture → The short version: connect your source to a DeckLink card, choose the input once, and watch. SDR, HDR10, HLG and Dolby Vision are recognised automatically, and a brief dropout reconnects itself. What the setup looks like Install Blackmagic's Desktop Video runtime and a DeckLink card. The runtime comes from Blackmagic's support portal; Unplugged does not bundle it. Connect the source to the card. A PC, camera, games console or AVR output that is not HDCP-protected. Run Unplugged in Video Processor mode. It opens the port, identifies the signal and presents it full-screen with your picture applied. File playback needs no capture card. The card is only for live HDMI. The signal must be unencrypted. DeckLink inputs do not accept HDCP-encrypted HDMI, and Unplugged does not decrypt or bypass HDCP. Use sources you are authorized to capture. SOURCE unencrypted HDMI DECKLINK capture UNPLUGGED tone map + grade DISPLAY projector / TV The live path: HDMI in, processed on the PC, GPU out to the display. The signal is recognised automatically Every port on every card is listed with a live badge: locked with SDR, HDR PQ or HDR HLG, or no signal. Dolby Vision over HDMI is recognised as its own case — profile 7 and profile 8 — rather than being read as plain SDR. HDR10 static metadata (MaxCLL, MaxFALL and the mastering display) is read from the card when the source carries it. The Info panel reports what was found, and the tone curve uses it. Source Signal Camera DeckLink Quad PCIe · HDMI Locked · HDR PQ Games console DeckLink Quad PCIe · HDMI Locked · SDR PC output DeckLink Quad PCIe · HDMI No signal It reconnects itself Capture is automatic. Plug a source in, unplug it, or let it renegotiate from SDR to HDR mid-session, and the picture follows without intervention. Brief dropouts wait out a grace window. A source changing format does not bounce you to a spinner. Format changes are followed, not fought. SDR, HDR10, HLG and Dolby Vision over HDMI each get the right treatment. Ports can be named. “Camera”, “Console”, “PC” — the name is yours and appears everywhere the port does. Inputs switch live. Clicking a row restarts capture on the new port; nothing else about the session changes. Built for live, not files A file can be buffered ahead. A live source cannot. The capture path is deliberately pull-based: No read-ahead cache. A demuxer running ahead is the same as buffering, and it is latency you cannot spend. No long probe before the first frame. Live input is not seekable; there is nothing to learn by waiting. Late frames are dropped, not queued. If the consumer falls behind wall clock, the queue does not grow until the picture lags the sound. A capture ring sized for 4K. The default buffer in a naive path overflows on a 4K HDR signal. Unplugged sizes it for the bitrate. These are implementation choices inside the FFmpeg DeckLink path, not settings you have to tune. They are listed because the source is public and the reasoning is part of the product. The same picture for live and files The live path and the file path meet the same video renderer, the same tone curves, the same display target and the same calibration LUT. A console and a film on disk are graded by the same code. Requirements: Windows 10/11 x64, Blackmagic's Desktop Video runtime, a Blackmagic DeckLink card for live HDMI (Quad PCIe and Mini Recorder 4K confirmed), and the GPU output connected to your display. The HDMI source must be unencrypted (non-HDCP); Unplugged does not decrypt or bypass HDCP. Dolby Vision in files (profile 5) is not supported in media player mode; Dolby Vision over HDMI is. title: Fill a wide screen without cropping — unplugged
text: unplugged / Scope screens Scope screens and projectors No black bars. No cropped picture. Fill a 2.39:1 scope screen without throwing away the edges. Unplugged shares the stretch across both axes, so the correction is spread out and faces near the edge keep their shape. Download free Then calibrate the panel → Every option has a trade-off Stretching evenly breaks shapes. Warping only the horizontal axis bends faces near the edges. Cropping throws picture away. Non-linear stretch trades a measured amount of the first two for the bars, and lets you decide how much. 16:9 PANEL BARS 2.39:1 PICTURE SHARED CORRECTION 12% VERTICAL + 12% HORIZONTAL Illustrative: sharing a 24% correction across both axes instead of spending it on one. The short version: choose how much of the black bars to remove, choose whether the stretch goes sideways, up-and-down or both, and protect the centre of the picture. The Warp/Crop readout tells you what the correction is costing. New in 2.1.0: NLS is set-and-forget. Auto handles clean 16:9 and scope content as well as letterboxed sources; Post NLS X/Y crop trims each axis after the stretch; scope-to-IMAX transitions are tracked per frame. Why both axes? A 2.39:1 film shown on a 16:9 panel needs roughly 24% more picture height to lose the bars. Horizontal-only NLS spends all of that in the width, which is why faces near the edges bend. Unplugged can split the same correction between the axes. At a 50/50 split, that 24% becomes about 12% up-and-down and 12% sideways. The bars are gone and each axis carries half the distortion. The exact ratio is yours to set. The controls, in plain terms Bars removed 0–100% · how much of the letterbox the picture grows into. It controls every fill mode; 0 is the film at its own aspect, 100 fills the screen. Half the bars costs half the distortion. Axis Horizontal (default) · Vertical · Split. Split uses the percentage below to share the correction. Vertical and split can elongate vertical detail. Split The share each axis takes. 50% is an even split. Max distortion 100–150% · caps the warp per axis in both directions. Whatever the warp refuses is covered by cropping the axis that has slack. Fill mode Auto · Stretch · Crop · Off. Auto fills up to the fill limit; Stretch never crops; Crop spends the bars; Off returns the film to its own aspect. Fill limit The largest correction Auto will fill with. Lock band Keeps one shape for titles that switch aspect mid-film, such as IMAX sequences. Centre protection Up to 90% · keeps a uniform, undistorted band around the middle and pushes the correction into the rim. Post NLS X / Y crop Per-axis crop after stretching. It covers the whole frame, including bars, and applies in real time. Try it live Every control applies as you move it, including on a paused frame, so you can judge the correction on a face rather than on motion. N toggles the stretch on and off for an A/B. The Info panel's Warp / Crop row reports what the current settings are actually costing, so “why does it look like that?” has a number next to it. One honest limit Both axes are being resampled, so with strong stretch fine text can look slightly soft. Lower the strength or raise centre protection if it bothers you. This is the honest cost of filling the screen without cropping, not a defect that a later setting hides. During a scope-to-IMAX transition, at least one IMAX frame can still use aspect-ratio NLS. The per-frame band tracking removes the stale-crop drop-outs; this single-frame case is the remaining limit. Measure the correction, then make it. title: Picture calibration for your projector or TV — unplugged
text: unplugged / Calibration Calibration A picture tuned to your screen. Tell Unplugged what your projector or TV can actually do — measured white, measured black and peak brightness — then apply a calibration LUT as the final polish. Download free The tone mapper → The short version: measure your screen once, enter its white, black and peak brightness, and load a calibration file if you have one. Every film is then mapped into what your projector or TV can actually show. MEASURE measured values TARGET entered once LUT optional .cube DISPLAY your screen Measure once, enter the target once, then the grade maps into your screen. Three numbers, set once Your display target is not a look. It is a description of the screen: where white sits, how bright the peak is, and how dark black actually goes. Set it from a measurement and leave it. Every tone curve and every source is mapped into it. SDR display nits 25–400, default 80. The measured SDR white of your display. A TV in a bright room is typically 100–200; a projector in a dark room 40–80. The AVSForum reference comparison used 120 nits. Static nits (max) 10–1000, default 1000. Your display's measured peak white in SDR mode — the destination the tone curve maps to. Display black 0–2, default 0. Your measured black level. OLED at true black stays 0; a projector measuring 0.3 gets 0.3, so shadow detail is not spent on a level the panel cannot show. Why the numbers matter Declared below your measurement, SDR white makes the picture run bright and the highlights pay: the shoulder clips sooner and sky detail goes first. Declared above it, films render dark with headroom unused. Brightness without lying about the panel is what Exposure is for. It works before the curve, in thirds of a stop, so the shoulder absorbs it instead of clipping. The display numbers stay measurements. Calibration is the final polish A DisplayCAL .cube loads into the app and is applied after tone mapping and grading. That ordering matters: the LUT corrects what the panel does to the picture, not what the film asked the panel to do. Separate from the tone curve. Change the source, the curve or the grade and the panel correction still applies. An enable toggle, not an unload. A/B the LUT without losing the loaded file. One display per LUT. Moving the PC to another panel means another measurement. Colour that fits your screen Colours can look garish not when they exceed the display gamut but when they sit exactly on its edge — the maximum for their lightness. Gamut capacity (709) lands each colour at a fraction of its own distance to the edge: 1.00 is off; 0.55 is the breathing room measured reference software leaves a deep-blue sky. Pale colours have long distances and stay untouched at any setting, so this cannot desaturate a whole film. It only relaxes colours crowded against the edge. Smooth away the steps HDR tone mapping down to an 8-bit SDR signal creates steps in slow gradients: sky fades, dark walls, the bloom around a lamp. Deband flattens each band edge and covers the work with fine grain. Deband On by default. Turn it off only if you want to keep the grain exactly as encoded. Threshold 0–256, default 32. How small a gradient step is treated. Range 1–64, default 16. How wide an area is blended per band. Iterations 1–4, default 1. Two is usually the honest maximum. Grain 0–128, default 24. The noise that hides the blending; matching real film grain is the target. Adaptive sharpen is the other finishing pass: it measures each edge against its local neighbourhood and limits itself, so it adds detail without white halos. It is off by default because clean 4K rarely needs it. How to measure Measure the panel. Use a colorimeter and DisplayCAL, in the display mode you actually watch in. Enter the three numbers. SDR white, peak white and black go into the Display Target section once. Do not re-enter them per film. Export a .cube. Load it in the calibration row; the LUT is applied as the final pass. A/B it. Use the enable toggle on a scene you know. If the LUT is doing its job, the difference should be in the panel's error, not in the film's look. Keep the jobs separate. If one film looks wrong, reach for Exposure or the curve, not the display target. If every film looks wrong the same way, the display target or the LUT is the suspect. Measure once. Watch everything. title: Content protection and HDCP — unplugged
text: unplugged / Content protection HDCP and DRM Content protection, stated plainly. Unplugged is a video processor and media player, not a DRM circumvention tool. The short version: Unplugged does not decrypt, strip or bypass HDCP or any other content protection. It works only with unencrypted HDMI signals the source already provides, and with content you are authorized to access. What Unplugged does Processes an unencrypted HDMI signal. A DeckLink input receives the signal, and Unplugged applies tone mapping, the Zion Grade and calibration to it. Plays files you already have. The media player decodes local MKV, MP4 and similar files with the same picture pipeline. Leaves content protection alone. It handles the signal as the source provides it. It does not negotiate, remove or alter content protection. What it does not do It does not decrypt or strip HDCP. There is no bypass, no decryption key and no “remove HDCP” feature. It does not remove DRM from files. It plays files that are already playable; it is not a decryption or ripping tool. It does not play commercial disc images. ISO and BDMV folder/playlist playback are not supported. It does not support protected commercial content. Commercial disc and streaming content is typically HDCP-protected and will not pass through a DeckLink input. What that means for your setup The HDMI source must already output an unencrypted signal. Sources that enforce HDCP will show no picture. That is a property of the input path and of the source, not something Unplugged can or will change. Use content you are authorized to access. Typical examples are your own camera output, a PC desktop or application, a game capture path where the platform permits it, and home video you own. The media player is for files you already have the right to play. If a source shows no picture The most likely cause is an HDCP-protected source. Unplugged cannot help bypass it, and support cannot provide instructions for doing so. Choose an unencrypted source, or use the media player for a file you already own. Why the limitation exists Blackmagic DeckLink inputs accept unencrypted HDMI only. Unplugged is built on that input path and does not add circumvention around it. Respecting content protection is a product requirement, not a missing feature. Back to the picture. Free · GPL-3.0 · Windows 10/11 x64 Download free
